twist.question: A mountain range runs from north to south. The wind blows from the NORTH, along the mountains, not across them. Which side is wetter?

options.text: About the same on both sides

twist.reason: The air isn't pushed up the slopes, so neither side gets the extra rain.

faq.a: Higher up, there's less air pressing down, so rising air spreads out, and spreading air cools.

faq.q: Does it ever rain in Pune?
faq.a: Yes, in the monsoon, just much less than in Mumbai.
A long line of hills and mountains along India's west coast. In Maharashtra they're called the Sahyadri.

knowledgePack: When moist wind meets a mountain, it is forced up the windward slope. Rising air cools, vapour condenses into clouds, and rain falls, mostly on the windward side and near the top. After crossing the top, the air sinks down the leeward side and warms up as it sinks, so clouds evaporate and little rain falls: a rain shadow. Taller mountains cause more lift and a stronger rain shadow. The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) do this to the south-west monsoon: Mumbai on the windward side gets about 2,000 to 2,500 mm a year; Pune on the leeward side gets about 700 mm. If the wind blows along a range rather than across it, there is little lifting. If the wind comes from dry land, there is little rain anywhere.

labChallenges.text: With the wind from the land, can you make lots of rain anywhere?
labChallenges.reason: Wind from the land is dry. No water, no rain, whatever the mountain does.

labChallenges.text: Make both cities get the same rain.

mission.text: On a drive to Lonavala or Pune in the monsoon, look out of the window. Where are the clouds thickest: on the Mumbai side, or after the ghats? Take a grown-up with you.
mission.debrief: You've seen a rain shadow with your own eyes.
